title: Find the Duplicate Number — Floyd's on index→value mapping.
shortTitle: Find the Duplicate Number — Floyd's on Index-to-Value Mapping

s1_definition.profdef: Given an array of n+1 integers where every value is between 1 and n, exactly one value is duplicated, and the task is to find it without modifying the array and using constant extra space. Treating each value as a pointer to the next index forms a linked list with a cycle whose entry is the duplicate, so Floyd's two-phase cycle detection finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India has a list of branch codes where one code was accidentally entered twice, and the array is read-only. Rajesh treats each slot's value as an arrow pointing to another slot; because the duplicate makes two arrows land on the same slot, the arrows form a loop, and the slot where the loop begins is the repeated code.
s1_definition.oneliner: Follow values as next-index pointers; the duplicate creates a cycle, and Floyd's algorithm finds the cycle's entry, which is the duplicate.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Given an array of n+1 integers where every value is between 1 and n, exactly one value is duplicated, and the task is to find it without modifying the array and using constant extra space. Treating each value as a pointer to the next index forms a linked list with a cycle whose entry is the duplicate, so Floyd's two-phase cycle detection finds it in O(n) time and O(1) space.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India has a list of branch codes where one code was accidentally entered twice, and the array is read-only. Rajesh treats each slot's value as an arrow pointing to another slot; because the duplicate makes two arrows land on the same slot, the arrows form a loop, and the slot where the loop begins is the repeated code.

**One line to remember:** Follow values as next-index pointers; the duplicate creates a cycle, and Floyd's algorithm finds the cycle's entry, which is the duplicate.

sections.s2_technical:
Define the successor of position `i` as `a[i]`, so moving from index `i` goes to index `a[i]`. Since every value is in the range 1 to n and there are n+1 slots, this mapping always stays within bounds and, because one value repeats, two different indices point to the same next index, which forms a cycle. The entry node of that cycle is the duplicated value.

Phase one runs Floyd starting from index 0: `slow = a[slow]` once and `fast = a[a[fast]]` twice until they meet. Phase two resets one pointer to 0 and advances both by one step (`slow = a[slow]`, `finder = a[finder]`) until they meet; the meeting index is the duplicate. A code snippet: `int findDup(int[] a) { int slow = a[0], fast = a[a[0]]; while (slow != fast) { slow = a[slow]; fast = a[a[fast]]; } int f = 0; while (f != slow) { f = a[f]; slow = a[slow]; } return f; }`.

The reason the cycle entry equals the duplicate is the same algebra as Linked List Cycle II: the distance equality from the two-to-one speed ratio makes the second phase converge exactly at the loop entry, and here that entry is the value two indices point into, which is the repeated number. The array is never modified and only two integer pointers are used.

A senior nuance is why obvious alternatives are rejected: sorting modifies the array or needs a copy, a hash set uses linear space, and the clever negation trick mutates the input. The Floyd mapping is the unique approach that satisfies both the read-only and constant-space constraints. It requires that values are in 1 to n so that no value equals an index you start outside of; starting slow at `a[0]` avoids the self-loop at index 0.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India loads a read-only array of branch routing codes in which exactly one code was duplicated by a data-entry error, and the validation service must identify the repeated code without altering the array and without extra memory. This is exactly how Find the Duplicate works — the duplicate is the cycle entry in the index-to-value mapping.

Problem 2 — The array is shared and immutable in this path, so sorting, a hash set, or the negation trick are all disallowed, leaving Floyd's mapping as the correct method.

The code shows a `RoutingCodeValidator` with `findDuplicate`, a demo on a routing-code array with one repeat, and the duplicate value.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: codes [1, 3, 4, 2, 3, 5], where value 3 appears at index 1 and index 4.

Step 1: Phase one begins. slow starts at a[0] which is 1. fast starts at a[a[0]] which is a[1] equals 3. They differ.

Step 2: slow becomes a[1] equals 3; fast becomes a[a[3]]. a[3] is 2 and a[2] is 4, so fast is 4. Different. slow becomes a[3] equals 2; fast becomes a[a[4]]. a[4] is 3 and a[3] is 2, so fast is 2. Now slow equals fast at 2, the meeting point.

Step 3: Phase two begins. finder starts at 0 while slow stays at 2. Both advance one step. finder becomes a[0] equals 1; slow becomes a[2] equals 4. Different.

Step 4: finder becomes a[1] equals 3; slow becomes a[4] equals 3. Now finder equals slow at 3.

Step 5: The convergence value 3 is the duplicate, exactly the code that was entered twice. The array was never modified and only integer pointers were used. The method returns 3.

```
2026-10-26 21:00:03 WARNING Duplicate detected: 3
2026-10-26 21:00:03 INFO    Duplicated routing code: 3
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Find the Duplicate Number gives me an array of n plus one integers whose values all lie between 1 and n, with exactly one value repeated, and asks me to find that value without modifying the array and in constant space. The key trick is to treat each value as a pointer to the next index, so moving from a position goes to the position named by its value. Because there are more slots than distinct values and one value repeats, two different positions point to the same next index, which forms a cycle, and the entry node of that cycle is the duplicated value.

That reframing lets me use Floyd's two-phase cycle detection. In phase one I advance a slow pointer by one hop and a fast pointer by two hops through this value-as-index mapping until they meet. In phase two I reset one pointer to the start and advance both by a single hop until they meet again, and the position where they converge is the duplicate. The correctness is the same distance equality as Linked List Cycle II, falling out of the two-to-one speed ratio.

The reason I reach for this specific method is the pair of constraints. Sorting would modify the array or need a copy, a hash set would use linear extra memory, and the negation trick mutates the input, so all three are disallowed when the array must stay read-only and memory must be constant. Floyd's mapping is the one approach that satisfies both, and starting the slow pointer at the first value rather than at index zero avoids the self-loop at position zero.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this in the routing-code validation service. A read-only array of branch routing codes had exactly one code duplicated by a data-entry error, and the service had to identify it without altering the shared array and without extra memory, which ruled out sorting, a hash set, and in-place marking. Explaining the value-as-pointer reframing, the two-phase Floyd detection, and why the constraints force this method shows the interviewer I can see a hidden cycle-detection problem inside an array question.
